items.title: Ecuador ENSO Floods 2026 - DREF Operational Update (MDREC032)
items.author: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies
items.content:
Country: Ecuador
Source: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies

Please refer to the attached file.

Description of the Event

Date of event

01-11-2026

What happened, where and when?

On 1 November 2026, heavy and persistent rainfall associated with the ongoing El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) phenomenon triggered flooding, river overflows, landslides and mudslides across several areas of Ecuador, causing damage to housing, livelihoods, road infrastructure, water systems, health facilities, educational establishments and other essential services. The impacts were particularly severe in the provinces of Esmeraldas, Guayas, El Oro, Galápagos, Santa Elena, Los Ríos, Manabí, Bolívar and Santo Domingo de los Tsáchilas. As of 3 November 2026, more than 55,000 people and over 12,000 homes had been affected, while damage to transportation networks, water systems and basic services further increased humanitarian needs and access constraints in affected communities.

The emergency occurred within the context of a strengthening ENSO event. Oceanic and atmospheric monitoring conducted by the National ERFEN Committee identified elevated ocean heat content extending toward the eastern Pacific, positive sea-level anomalies of up to 45 cm in the central-eastern Pacific, 40 cm around the Galápagos Islands and 35 cm along the Ecuadorian coast, the propagation of warm Kelvin waves and a deepened thermocline. Sea surface temperature anomalies in the Niño 1+2 region reached up to +5.2°C above average, creating favourable conditions for above-normal rainfall and increasing the likelihood of severe hydrometeorological impacts across the country.

Anticipating these conditions, the Government of Ecuador progressively strengthened preparedness measures and, on 29 August 2026, the National Secretariat for Risk Management (SNGR) declared a nationwide Red Alert through Resolution No. SNGR-238-2026 due to the risk of flooding, landslides and other hydrometeorological hazards. Based on the forecasts and available lead time, the Ecuadorian Red Cross activated its ENSO National Contingency Plan and launched an Imminent DREF operation focused on anticipatory actions in Esmeraldas, Guayas, Los Ríos and Santo Domingo de los Tsáchilas, including community preparedness, strengthening of Early Warning Systems, temporary protection of homes, safeguarding of water systems, risk communication and institutional readiness measures.

During October and early November, forecasted impacts progressively materialized and expanded geographically, resulting in recurrent flooding, river overflows, landslides and disruptions to essential services across multiple provinces. Assessments and official reports indicate that the scale, severity and duration of impacts now exceed the scope originally envisaged under the 45-day Imminent DREF operation, requiring a transition to a Response DREF. The operation will support affected populations through emergency response activities while maintaining anticipatory actions in at-risk communities where forecast impacts have not yet materialized.

According to forecasts issued by INAMHI, the ERFEN Committee and NOAA, which estimates a probability of more than 90 per cent that the current ENSO event could reach a very strong intensity, above-average rainfall is expected to persist during the coming months and into the 2026-2027 rainy season. Additional flooding, river overflows, landslides and damage to critical infrastructure and essential services remain likely, particularly in coastal provinces, low-lying areas and communities exposed to recurrent flooding and territorial isolation.

items.title: Yemen - Displacement Caused by Escalation in Western Yemen - Update #19 (18 November 2026)
items.author: International Organization for Migration
items.content:
Country: Yemen
Source: International Organization for Migration

Please refer to the attached file.

IOM Yemen DTM continues to record displacement caused by the escalation in western Yemen. As of 17 November 2026, IOM Yemen DTM recorded an increase of 9,281 individual IDPs compared to the figure presented in the RDT report distributed on 16 November 2026, bringing displacement between 1 August and 17 November to approximately 356,602 individuals (59,426 households)1. This brings the cumulative number recorded since the escalation began in June 2026 to 357,658 individuals (59,602 households).

The largest concentration of displaced people was reported in Ta’iz Governorate, hosting 145,344 individuals (41%), followed by Lahj Governorate with 95,580 individuals (27%), and Aden Governorate with 71,706 individuals (20%). Additional displacement was recorded in Abyan with 17,208 individuals (5%); Al Hodeidah with 8,244 individuals (2%)2; Shabwah with 6,183 individuals (2%); Ma’rib with 4,104 individuals (1%); Hadramawt with 3,576 individuals (1%); Al Maharah with 3,096 individuals (less than 1%); and Ad Dali’ with 2,617 individuals (less than 1%).

items.content:

According to the latest available figures from the Turkish Presidency of Migration Management (PMM), there are more than 3.6 million foreign nationals present in Turkish territory, 2.3 million of whom are seeking international protection. Most are Syrians (2,206,483 individuals) who are granted temporary protection status. Another group of foreigners are international protection applicants and holders mainly from Iraq, Afghanistan, the Islamic Republic of Iran and Ukraine. According to United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), there were 145,155 refugees and asylum-seekers in Türkiye as of 2026.

items.title: Ethiopia — Flow Monitoring Snapshot Report (1 - 30 June 2026)
items.author: International Organization for Migration
items.content:
Countries: Ethiopia, Djibouti, Kenya, Somalia, Sudan, Uganda, Yemen
Source: International Organization for Migration

Please refer to the attached file.

In Ethiopia, FM data is gathered in five of the country’s land crossborder points, namely: Dawele, Galafi, Metema, Moyale and Tog Wajale FMPs. In Kurmuk, data collection has been interrupted since 3 February 2026 due to insecurity in the border area.

Between 1 and 30 June 2026, a total of 107,719 movements were identified across the assessed five FMPs in Ethiopia, highlighting continued population mobility along key migration routes.

Outgoing movements (58,188 individuals) accounted for the largest share of observed flows (54.0%), whereas incoming movements (49,531 individuals) accounted for 46.0 per cent of observed flows. This indicates that more individuals exited the monitored areas compared to those that entered.

items.title: WHO Weekly Situation Update on Ongoing Health Emergency Events in South Sudan - Week #46, Date: 9 – 15 Nov 2026
items.author: World Health Organization
items.content:
Countries: South Sudan, Democratic Republic of the Congo, Kenya, Nigeria
Source: World Health Organization

Please refer to the attached file.

PRIORITY ACTIONS

  • Sustain BVD preparedness as the DRC outbreak reaches 11,376 cases and 5,568 deaths (CFR 48.9%); maintain PoE screening (83,826 events over 14–16 Nov) and screen air arrivals at Juba International Airport. Strengthen cross-border surveillance on the Yei–Morobo–Kaya corridor given spread to Watsa (Haut-Uélé) and cases in Aru and Ariwara; sustain alert investigation and testing in Yei, Morobo and Yambio.
  • Sustain cholera response in Fangak and Renk (Rubkona and Mayom have had no cases since 30 October) and investigate the Aweil West (Wedweil) cluster of 67 mostly untested cases; drive 100% RDT testing toward the earliest end-of-outbreak declaration (8 December).
  • Deliver the Round 2 polio NIDs (17–20 November; 87% readiness) and sustain measles response; the Magwi reactive campaign is completed (12,953 under-fives), with Malakal and Canal/Pigi campaigns being planned.
  • Investigate the six suspected human anthrax cases in Jur River (Western Bahr el Ghazal) and sustain Guinea worm surveillance (no human or animal case in 2026); maintain malaria response (48,675 cases, 47% below 2025).

items.creator: Health Cluster
items.title: Conflict Escalation in Yemen - Situation Report #12 (Reporting period: 11 – 17 November 2026 | Issued: 17 November 2026)
items.author: Health Cluster
items.content:
Country: Yemen
Sources: Health Cluster, World Health Organization

Please refer to the attached file.

Key Highlights

  • Casualties continue, with Marib and Lahj carrying the burden. The HEOC count reached 12,779 (10,519 injured, 2,260 deaths) by 16 November, +1,024 in eight days. The daily average fell to ~128 from ~225, but reporting was incomplete (58–92% a day, none for 9–10 November), so the figures are a minimum. Between 11 and 15 November, Marib reported 266 casualties and 49 deaths and Lahj 234 casualties; Al-Dhale’e still has no funded WHO-supported trauma deployment.
  • The front line is moving towards Aden. Front lines moved rapidly through Lahj and are approaching Aden, which hosts the main referral hospitals, the Health Emergency Operations Centre and the warehouse supplying the response. Further movement may change casualty flows and displacement, disrupt referral and supply routes, and require WHO and partners to adapt their operations.
  • Measles–rubella campaign reached 92.3% of target. MoPHP results show 883,896 children aged 6–59 months vaccinated and 741,713 given vitamin A (77.5%). Al-Mahrah (61%) and Socotra (78%) fell short and 73,300 children were not reached. WHO-supported teams vaccinated 6,007 displaced children in five IDP camps in Aden and Lahj.
  • Displacement continues to be at about 3,150 households a week. IOM DTM has recorded 347,321 people displaced since 1 August, including 18,780 in the past week, of whom 55% went to Lahj and 30% went to Taiz.
  • Cholera is falling in the five most-affected governorates, but a complex outbreak is growing in Tarim. Suspected cases fell from 638 (W40) to 321 (W45). Tarim (Hadramout Al-Wadi) has reported 172 cases of acute diarrhea since W43, 78 RDT-positive and 22 culture-confirmed, with both suspected food and water. A diarrhea treatment center is being set up.
  • Fuel and medical supplies are critically short in Taiz. Severe shortages of fuel, surgical supplies and anesthesia medicines are disrupting emergency services, including operating theatres and oxygen generation for intensive care units, and hospitals cannot sustain the continuous pressure. WHO delivered 19.6 MT of medicines and supplies to three facilities, and IRY and FMF plan to support two city hospitals.
  • Shortages are also reported across the front line. Health facilities in areas under the control of the de facto authorities are reported to be short of medical and surgical supplies. Alternative delivery routes and access negotiations are needed to reach hospitals on both sides.
  • The trauma referral pathway has critical gaps. Only four of the 35 planned trauma stabilization points are funded, none of them in Aden or in the part of Lahj towards which the front line is moving, and referral dispatch is unfunded. Burn cases are rising, yet hospitals can offer little beyond initial stabilization and wound dressing. Mental health and psychosocial support and rehabilitation remain the weakest links, leaving patients without continuity of care.
  • Funding remains the binding constraint. All 32 WHO-supported trauma deployments are funded only until January 2027. WHO’s third CERF request is being consolidated at US$2.4 million, including sites, mobile teams and supplies proposed by UNICEF and IOM.

items.title: Somalia Weekly Weather Forecast - Valid From 18 - 24 Nov 2026
items.author: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations
items.content:
Country: Somalia
Source: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations

Please refer to the attached file.

Review Summary:

  • Significant local rains in the south, little rain in the centre and north. During 10–16 November, Bualle recorded 159.9 mm, Balcad 115.0 mm and Awdheegle 88.4 mm, while most stations in Bay, Hiraan and the centre recorded little or no rain. In the north, Las Dacawo recorded 50.0 mm and Elafweyn 31.5 mm. Satellite estimates (IMERG, 11–17 November) indicate 30–55 mm over Lower Juba and parts of Middle Juba and Gedo.
  • By 16 November, 37 stations, 33 of them with a Deyr normal above 15 mm, had already received their full Deyr normal, including Baidoa (405.5 mm, 176% of the Deyr normal), Galkacyo (253.5 mm, 390%), Awdheegle (265.2 mm, 169%) and Bualle (240.9 mm, 148%), which passed its normal this week. Borama (16%), Burao (21%), Luuq (25%) and Mogadishu (27%) remain far below normal.
  • River levels are rising slightly on the upper Shabelle and the Juba but remain well below flood-risk levels. Belet Weyne rose from 2.90 m on 15 November to 3.76 m today, 2.74 m below its moderate flood-risk level. Jowhar (2.90 m) and Bulo Burti (2.30 m) are falling, and Dollow (2.86 m) and Luuq (2.78 m) are rising slowly.
  • Flood water in Jowhar district is receding. Satellite images show about 55 km² of flood water in Jowhar district, down from about 87 km² last week. Radio Ergo callers (5–11 November) reported flash floods that drowned livestock at Garadag in Sanaag and a death in stagnant flood water in Hirshabelle, while many callers in the south and centre welcomed the rains and said they had not seen the floods mentioned in the alerts.

items.author: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies
items.content:
Countries: Central African Republic, Democratic Republic of the Congo
Source: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies

Please refer to the attached file.

Description of the Event

Date of event

17-05-2026

What happened, where and when?

Between 15 and 18 May 2026, the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) declared an outbreak of Ebola Virus Disease (EVD) caused by the Bundibugyo strain as a major public health emergency. This declaration was rapidly echoed by the World Health Organization (WHO) and the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC).

At that time, the outbreak mainly affected three provinces in the DRC, namely Ituri, North Kivu, and South Kivu. As of 18 June 2026, a total of 33 health zones had reported confirmed cases, distributed as follows:

21 out of 36 health zones (58.3%) in Ituri;
11 out of 34 health zones (32.4%) in North Kivu;
1 health zone in South Kivu.

These figures confirmed that Ituri Province remained the epicentre of the outbreak.

According to WHO data available on 18 June 2026, the DRC had recorded 896 confirmed EVD cases, including 208 deaths and 78 recoveries. Cross-border transmission had also been reported in Uganda, with 19 confirmed cases, including two deaths and seven recoveries.

Although the Central African Republic (CAR) had not reported any confirmed EVD cases at that time, the country remained at high risk of disease importation due to its proximity to the affected areas of the DRC. This outbreak, the seventeenth recorded in the DRC and the second associated with the Bundibugyo strain, had progressively expanded towards provinces located near the CAR border, notably Haut-Uélé. Available epidemiological information indicated a high likelihood of ongoing undetected transmission in this province, which serves as an important population movement corridor towards the border provinces of Bas-Uélé and South Ubangi.

Furthermore, several public health alerts had been reported in areas close to the CAR border, including:

The report of a death associated with a suspected viral haemorrhagic fever in Libenge Health Zone, South Ubangi Province, which hosts Central African refugees;
A report dated 18 June 2026 from the Chief Medical Officer of Yakoma Health Zone regarding a suspected EVD case in a locality bordering Ouango-Gambo Health District in CAR.

In this context, the combination of proximity to areas of probable transmission, intense cross-border population movements, repeated epidemiological alerts, and limited preparedness capacities fully justified the activation of a DREF preparedness operation. The operation aimed to anticipate and reduce the risk of EVD introduction and spread in CAR through proactive preparedness, community-based surveillance, and community engagement activities.

However, the epidemiological situation evolved in a concerning manner, with the outbreak progressively spreading to provinces that share a direct border with CAR. In August 2026, Bas-Uélé Province, which borders CAR, reported its first confirmed EVD case in Buta Health Zone, becoming the sixth affected province in the DRC. The confirmed case was linked to travel from Haut-Uélé Province, highlighting the persistent risk associated with population movements between affected areas and border districts in CAR.

As of 19 August 2026, the DRC had reported 5,208 confirmed cases and 2,476 deaths, compared to 896 cases and 208 deaths on 18 June 2026. In addition, 84 per cent of identified contacts were under follow-up. On the same date, another confirmed EVD case was reported in Viadana Health Zone, Bas-Uélé Province, in close proximity to the Haut-Mbomou, Mbomou, and Basse-Kotto health districts of the Central African Republic.

The progression of the outbreak is particularly alarming. While three provinces and 33 health zones were affected as of 18 June 2026, the situation had expanded to six provinces and 55 affected health zones by 19 August 2026. This continued geographical expansion brought the outbreak significantly closer to the CAR border and substantially increased the risk of virus introduction into the country.

Since the launch of the preparedness operation, sixty-four (64) suspected EVD cases have been reported and investigated in CAR. All laboratory test results returned negative for Ebola Virus Disease.

By the end of October 2026, the regional situation had deteriorated further. Most DRC provinces bordering CAR were affected by EVD, including Bas-Uélé, Haut-Uélé, South Ubangi, and North Ubangi. Geographical proximity, combined with the strong historical and family ties between communities living along the Ubangi River, facilitates significant formal and informal cross-border population movements.

As of 25 October 2026, the epidemiological situation in the DRC reported:

10,060 cumulative cases;
4,887 deaths;
2,684 recoveries;
1,008 patients admitted to treatment centres;
a case fatality rate of 48.6%;
a contact tracing rate of 81.6%.

These cases were distributed across eight provinces and 66 health zones or health districts.

At the same time, the Central African Republic has progressively strengthened its preparedness capacity. The national preparedness level increased from 42 per cent at the beginning of the operation to 68 per cent during the latest assessment conducted at the end of August 2026. The 30-day acceleration plan validated in early October 2026 aims to raise this level to 95 per cent.

As part of this acceleration plan, the Incident Management System has been decentralized to bring coordination closer to the highest-risk regions and their border health districts. Efforts are underway to make Ebola Treatment Centres fully operational in Obo, Bangassou, the Bimbo University Teaching Hospital, and PK24. Surveillance at points of entry has been reinforced, as have risk communication and community engagement activities, under the leadership of the Minister of Health.

The Central African Red Cross (CRCA), which leads the Safe and Dignified Burials pillar, has trained fifteen teams of ten volunteers each to ensure adequate coverage of high-risk localities.

Finally, on 22 and 23 October 2026, CAR and the DRC met in Bangui for a cross-border coordination meeting aimed at strengthening information sharing, exchanging experiences, and improving joint preparedness measures to prevent and control any potential spread of the outbreak in health districts on both sides of the border.

items.title: World: Ending violence against children: From commitment to reality
items.author: UN Children's Fund
items.content:
Country: World
Source: UN Children's Fund

Please refer to the attached file.

Violence against children remains one of the most widespread violations of children’s rights worldwide. Despite global commitments to end all forms of violence against children, millions of children continue to experience violence across regions and income levels, revealing the persistent gap between commitment and reality.

This brief presents the latest available global estimates on violent discipline by caregivers in the home and sexual violence in childhood, drawing on evidence from both development and humanitarian contexts. The brief illustrates why accelerating progress towards SDG Target 16.2 remains an urgent priority and highlights the essential role of both universal and targeted prevention efforts and a strong, accessible social service workforce equipped with a package of evidence-based family support and child protection services.

Accelerating progress will require renewed political commitment, sustained investment, stronger child protection systems capable of delivering evidence-based services at scale in cooperation with allied services such as health, education, and justice, and the large-scale implementation of proven universal and targeted prevention interventions.

items.title: World: A record high of nearly one in four children now live in conflict zones - Save the Children report
items.author: Save the Children
items.content:
Country: World
Source: Save the Children

· Nearly one in four children worldwide live in conflict zones, new report finds

· Africa now accounts for 44% of children living near conflict worldwide, with an unprecedented two in five African children impacted

· Verified incidents of denial of humanitarian access against children have increased almost 16-fold in a decade to almost one an hour

AMMAN, 19 November 2026 – Almost one in four children worldwide are now living in conflict zones, the highest number since records began in 1990, according to a new Save the Children report.

The figure represents an increase of more than 50% in a decade, jumping from 378 million in 2015 to 589 million in 2025, according to the report Stop the War on Children: Changing the Odds, which draws on data from the Peace Research Institute Oslo (PRIO).

The report found that the share of the world’s children living in conflict zones more than doubled from about 10% in the mid-1990s to 23.4% in 2025.

Africa is home to the highest number of children living in conflict zones, accounting for about 260 million, or 44% of the global total. This is nearly a 20% increase from the 218 million children in Africa who lived in conflict zones in 2024.

Across Africa, the proportion of children living in conflict zones more than tripled from about one in eight children in 2010 to about two in five in 2025, the highest level ever recorded for the continent. This puts Africa on par with the Middle East, where both regions now have two in five children living in conflict zones.

Elsewhere, about one in four children (24.2%) in the Americas lived in conflict zones in 2025, one in seven (14.3%) in Asia, and nearly one in nine (10.6%) in Europe.

The report also examined United Nations verified grave violations against children in armed conflict between 2005 and 2025, including killing and maiming, recruitment by armed forces or groups, sexual violence, abduction, attacks on schools and hospitals, and denial of humanitarian access. These numbers represent the tip of the iceberg for grave violations against children, as most attacks on children go unverified, said Save the Children.

Killing and maiming accounted for the largest share of violations against children over the past two decades, with 171,712 cases verified since 2005. More than 70% of the cases were committed against children in five countries: the occupied Palestinian territory, Afghanistan, Somalia, Syria and Yemen.

The report also found that the fastest-growing grave violation against children is the denial of humanitarian aid, with verified incidents skyrocketing from 509 in 2015 to 8,322 in 2025, more than a 16-fold increase in a decade. This amounts to almost one verified incident of denial of humanitarian aid every hour, on average, in 2025. More than 70% of all verified aid denial last year took place against Palestinian children.

Denial of humanitarian access rose from just over 2% of all verified grave violations in 2015 to more than 21% in 2025, making it the second most frequently verified violation after killing and maiming.

Rape and other forms of sexual violence against children are widely underreported. Even so, the report found that 28,909 cases have been verified since reporting began. The Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) accounts for 12,698, or almost 44% of the total, followed by Somalia with 4,534 and Chad with 2,979. Together, the three countries account for around 70% of all verified cases.

In eastern DRC, 17-year-old Ana* experienced the devastating consequences of conflict after violence forced her family from their home. After months of displacement, they returned, only for armed men to break into their house, shoot Ana’s brother dead and rape her while other family members were assaulted.

“We had fled the war, but it came knocking at our door again. [When the attackers came to our home] I screamed; I begged for mercy… but no one listened. My brother was killed before my eyes. I was raped,” Ana said. “[Afterwards] the hardest part wasn’t the pain. It was people’s mockery. They pointed fingers at me, as if I were to blame for what had been done to me.”

The next morning, neighbours helped Ana reach a local health centre supported by Save the Children, where she received emergency medical care, including treatment to prevent pregnancy and sexually transmitted infections, as well as ongoing psychosocial support.

Gudrun Østby, Research Professor at PRIO, said: “We estimate that 589 million children were living close to armed conflict last year. These record-high figures are a stark reminder that conflict is devastating the daily lives, education, health and future prospects of hundreds of millions of children. Unless greater efforts are made to protect children in conflict settings, the consequences of today's wars will be felt for decades to come.”

Inger Ashing, CEO of Save the Children International, said:

“Almost one in four children around the world now lives in a conflict zone. What could be more important than their protection? The scale of this crisis is rapidly growing, and the systems meant to protect children are being pushed to breaking point.

“We're seeing aid weaponised, attacked and deliberately disrupted. Humanitarian organisations are denied access, funding is being slashed, and needs are outpacing our ability to reach every child in crisis. Meanwhile, parties to conflict continue to disregard the rules of war, while new military technologies are changing how wars are fought, increasing the risk further for children in conflict settings.

“Children’s rights and needs must be at the centre of decisions about war, peace and security. More than 20 years of monitoring violations have made the horrors children face visible and created opportunities to prevent further harm. This work must be protected, supported and translated into action.

"Parties to conflict must uphold the rules of war, and those responsible for violations must be held to account. But ensuring the protection of children isn’t only the responsibility of those fighting. States, donors and companies with leverage over perpetrators must use it, through diplomatic and political pressure. To truly change the odds for children living in conflict zones, we must put their protection first and work towards the peace they deserve.”

Save the Children is calling on parties to the conflict to uphold international humanitarian law, accounting for children’ distinct vulnerabilities, and to facilitate safe and unimpeded humanitarian relief to civilians. It is also urging governments to strengthen accountability for violations against children, implement international treaties and declarations that protect children and education in war zones, address the root causes of conflict and ensure children’s voices are heard in decisions affecting their futures.

In 2025, Save the Children worked in 107 countries, reaching more than 58.2 million people, including 37.8 million children. The child rights organisation also responded to 113 humanitarian crises in 63 countries, supporting over 24 million people, including 13.6 million children.

ENDS

Notes to Editor:

Read the full report here: https://resourcecentre.savethechildren.net/document/stop-the-war-on-children-changing-the-odds-2026

· The updated analysis on the number and share of children living in conflict zones is conducted by the Peace Research Institute Oslo (PRIO). The core dataset used to map conflict patterns in this report is the Uppsala Conflict Data Program’s Georeferenced Event Data Set (UCDP GED) until 2025. To estimate the number of children living in conflict areas, and populations more generally, PRIO integrated the UCDP conflict data with population data from CIESIN’s Gridded Population of the World (GPW) and from the UN World Population Prospects. PRIO uses UCDP’s definition of armed conflict: ‘armed force used by an organized actor against another organized actor, or against civilians, resulting in at least 25 battle-related deaths in one calendar year’. A ‘conflict zone’ is defined as an area within 50km of where one or more conflict incidents take place in a given year, within the borders of a country.

· The UN Security Council has identified six grave violations against children in situations of armed conflict: killing and maiming of children; recruitment or use of children by armed forces and groups; sexual violence against children; abduction of children; attacks against schools and hospitals; and denial of humanitarian access for children. These grave violations were defined on the basis of their egregious nature and their severe impact on children’s wellbeing.

· Stop the War on Children

Global Overview: El Niño is present. Abnormal Dryness and Drought conditions persist in East Africa, northwestern and southeastern Kazakhstan, and parts of Central America, Hispaniola, and Northern South America.

Africa Weather Hazards

Erratic rainfall has led to dryness in eastern Horn of Africa; high flood risks remain in many areas of Eastern Africa and Southern Africa.

1) Inundation persists in the Sudd Wetlands of South Sudan.

2) A large part of western Eastern Africa faces dryness due to persisting, below-average rainfall over the past 90 days. Southern and southeastern South Sudan and northern Uganda have already experienced deteriorated vegetation conditions, which have resulted in droughts in the region.

3) Flooding is likely to continue in Gemena of northwestern DRC, parts of Gabon, Congo, western DRC, along the Juba River in southern Somalia, the KwaZulu-Natal of eastern South Africa, and Eswatini as additional rainfall is forecast in each region during the next week.

4) High flooding risks also exist in southern Ethiopia, southern Kenya, northern and western Tanzania, westcentral Angola, north-central Mozambique, and central Madagascar due to the forecast, additional rainfall during the next week.

5) Southeastern Ethiopia and central Somalia face dryness due to poor rainfall over the past four weeks.

6) Hot conditions are predicted over parts of far western West Africa, Eastern Africa, and a wide area in central and eastern Southern Africa.

items.title: Anticipatory Action Activation: Anticipatory Action to mitigate the impacts of drought in Malawi (November 2026)
items.author: World Food Programme
items.content:
Country: Malawi
Source: World Food Programme

Please refer to the attached file.

In August 2026, the World Food Programme (WFP), in collaboration with the Government of Malawi, activated Anticipatory Action (AA) in Mangochi, Nsanje and Zomba districts, following forecasts of drought conditions during the 2026/27 agricultural season.

Malawi's reliance on rain-fed agriculture means rainfall deficit can quickly reduce harvests, incomes and food security.

The activation follows a Ready, Set and Go approach based on pre-agreed drought triggers. The readiness trigger was reached in July 2026 and the activation trigger in August 2026 following consecutive forecasts of drought conditions, providing lead time to deliver support before impacts are fully met.

The targeting approach combines food security information with drought-risk forecasts to prioritize support for households projected to face acute food insecurity (IPC Phase 3+) in the most affected areas. Assistance focuses on farming households with access to land and labour, recognizing that most vulnerable households retain productive capacity but struggle to achieve adequate harvests because of climatic shocks and resource constraints.

To address the anticipated impacts, WFP is implementing the following anticipatory actions:

  • Dissemination of early warning messages and climate advisories: Weather, agricultural, nutrition and hygiene messages will be disseminated through SMS, radio and community structures.
  • Provision of agricultural inputs: Distribution of drought-tolerant and early-maturing seed varieties and fertilizer to 9,051 households ahead of planting in December.
  • Distribution of anticipatory multipurpose cash assistance: Cash transfers of USD 130 will be distributed to the same households in January 2027 at peak lean season, helping them meet immediate needs while protecting productive investments.

Unlike traditional Lean Season Response assistance, which primarily addresses food consumption gaps, AA aims to protect both food security and agricultural production.

The 2026/27 activation builds on the successful 2025/26 AA intervention which was characterized by late onset of rainfall and midseason dry spells of more than 10 days, but not a severe drought.

Compared with households receiving traditional Lean Season Response food assistance, AA beneficiaries achieved improved food security, reduced reliance on negative coping strategies and substantially higher agricultural production.

In maize-growing districts, AA increased average maize harvests by approximately 1.2 metric tonnes per household. The intervention generated an estimated USD 569 in additional benefits per household, with every additional USD 1 invested generating USD 2.31 in benefits relative to the standard in-kind lean season assistance.

The expected outcomes of this intervention are improved household food security; reduced negative coping strategies; protection of productive assets and livelihoods; higher agricultural production and harvests; and reduced future humanitarian needs.

This anticipatory action activation is supported through USD 1.75 million in funding from Norway and USD 567,000 from Ireland.

items.title: Belize: Los países del MIRPS reafirman su compromiso con el fortalecimiento de los sistemas de protección, la promoción de soluciones duraderas y la generación de oportunidades de inclusión para personas con necesidades de protección
items.author: UN High Commissioner for Refugees
items.content:
Countries: Belize, Costa Rica, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, Mexico, Panama
Source: UN High Commissioner for Refugees

SAN SALVADOR – Los siete países que integran el Marco Integral Regional para la Protección y Soluciones (MIRPS) –Belice, Costa Rica, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, México y Panamá– concluyeron hoy la IX Reunión Anual del MIRPS con la adopción de la Declaración de San Salvador II, mediante la cual renovaron sus compromisos para fortalecer los sistemas nacionales de protección, ampliar las oportunidades de inclusión socioeconómica y avanzar en soluciones duraderas para personas con necesidades de protección y las comunidades que las acogen.

Durante el encuentro, celebrado bajo el liderazgo del Gobierno de El Salvador en su calidad de Presidencia Pro-Témpore 2026, autoridades de los países MIRPS, representantes de la Plataforma de Apoyo y socios estratégicos realizaron un balance de los avances alcanzados durante 2026 y examinaron las oportunidades y las prioridades que orientarán la cooperación regional en 2027. El diálogo destacó los resultados y buenas prácticas en materia de asilo, protección a nivel territorial, gobernabilidad local y medios de vida.

La Reunión Anual culminó con la adopción de la Declaración de San Salvador II, en la que los Estados acordaron promover procedimientos de asilo más accesibles, eficientes y de calidad, ampliar el acceso a empleo, educación y medios de vida, e incorporar enfoques de protección en las políticas de gestión del riesgo de desastres y adaptación al cambio climático.

Los países también destacaron la importancia de profundizar la cooperación con otros mecanismos regionales y fortalecer las alianzas con gobiernos locales, sociedad civil, organizaciones lideradas por personas refugiadas, academia, sector privado y actores del desarrollo, con el propósito de ampliar el alcance y la sostenibilidad de las respuestas. Asimismo, reconocieron el valor del MIRPS como una plataforma regional que permite promover respuestas coordinadas en beneficio de las personas con necesidades de protección y las comunidades de acogida.

La Organización de los Estados Americanos (OEA), que integra junto con ACNUR la Secretaría Técnica del MIRPS, destacó los avances del Fondo MIRPS, cuyos proyectos han beneficiado a más de 33.000 personas en la región, y agradeció las contribuciones de España, la República de Corea y Portugal. “El desplazamiento sigue afectando a personas y familias en todo nuestro hemisferio. Atender sus necesidades va más allá de brindar protección inmediata y requiere instituciones sólidas, políticas inclusivas y una cooperación regional que abra caminos hacia la estabilidad y las oportunidades. Estos principios guían la Agenda de Paz y Prosperidad para las Américas de la OEA. En nuestro trabajo con las personas desplazadas, esto significa acceso a la protección, la documentación, la educación y el empleo, así como oportunidades para desarrollar su autonomía y vivir con dignidad”, afirmó Albert R. Ramdin, Secretario General de la OEA, al destacar el compromiso de la Organización con la protección y la inclusión de las personas con necesidades de protección.

En el marco del 75.º aniversario de la Convención sobre el Estatuto de los Refugiados de 1951, ACNUR destacó la importancia de mantener el compromiso regional con la protección internacional. “La adopción de la Declaración de San Salvador II demuestra que los países de la región siguen apostando por la cooperación, la solidaridad y la responsabilidad compartida para responder al desplazamiento. A través del MIRPS, los Estados continúan transformando sus compromisos en acciones concretas para las personas refugiadas, desplazadas y las comunidades que las acogen", afirmó Isabel Márquez, Directora Regional de ACNUR para las Américas.

Los miembros de la Plataforma de Apoyo al MIRPS reafirmaron su compromiso de continuar acompañando los esfuerzos de los países mediante la cooperación técnica, la movilización de recursos y el fortalecimiento de alianzas estratégicas para apoyar la implementación de las prioridades nacionales y regionales, ampliar las oportunidades de protección y soluciones duraderas, y contribuir a la sostenibilidad de los esfuerzos impulsados por los Estados que integran este Mecanismo.

Al cierre de la IX Reunión Anual, El Salvador traspasó la Presidencia Pro-Témpore del MIRPS a Guatemala, que liderará el mecanismo durante 2027, en un año particularmente significativo en el que el MIRPS conmemorará su décimo aniversario.

A una década de la adopción de la Declaración de San Pedro Sula, este Mecanismo continúa consolidándose como una plataforma regional de cooperación, innovación y responsabilidad compartida que permite a los Estados avanzar conjuntamente en la protección, la inclusión y las soluciones para las personas refugiadas, desplazadas y otras personas con necesidades de protección internacional.

El Marco Integral Regional para la Protección y Soluciones (MIRPS) está integrado por Belice, Costa Rica, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, México y Panamá. Es un mecanismo regional para la aplicación del Pacto Mundial sobre los Refugiados que promueve la cooperación y la responsabilidad compartida en materia de prevención, protección y soluciones duraderas frente al desplazamiento. La Plataforma de Apoyo al MIRPS, creada en 2019, contribuye a movilizar recursos y cooperación internacional. ACNUR y la OEA, a través de su Departamento de Acceso a Derechos (DAR), integran la Secretaría Técnica del MIRPS y su Plataforma de Apoyo.

Para más información sobre este tema, favor de contactar:

  • En ACNUR: Melanie Gallant, gallant@unhcr.org
  • En la OEA: Nicole Levoyer, NLevoyer@oas.org
